title: Passover: the seder
hook: a meal in order, with matzah, bitter herbs, four cups and a story told to children

segments.voice: Yesterday, mishloach manot: food for friends on Purim, and gifts to the poor. Your line was give on the happy day. A month after Purim, the spring festival arrives. Day one hundred thirty-five.

It's the first night of Passover. The table is set for more people than usual, with extra chairs borrowed from the neighbors. There's a plate with strange things on it: a roasted bone, a bitter root, a sweet brown paste, a sprig of green, salt water. There's flat, crackly bread under a cloth. Everyone has a book in front of them. And before the main meal is served, which may be a long time from now, the youngest child at the table stands up, maybe a little nervous, and asks a question everyone has been waiting for: why is this night different from all other nights?
screen: `EXTRA CHAIRS, A STRANGE PLATE.` → `FLAT BREAD UNDER A CLOTH.` → `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?`

segments.voice: This meal is the seder. The word means order, because the evening follows fixed steps, fifteen of them in the traditional telling, from the first blessing over wine to the songs at the end. The book on the table is the Haggadah, which means the telling. Because at its heart, the seder is a story told out loud. The Torah commands it: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day, saying: It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." Notice: for me. Not for my ancestors. The Haggadah says each person should see themselves as if they personally came out of Egypt. Everything on the table helps tell it. Matzah, the flat bread, because they left in such a hurry the dough had no time to rise. Maror, bitter herbs, for the bitterness of slavery. Charoset, the sweet paste, looking like the mortar they used for bricks. Salt water, for tears. Four cups of wine, for the four promises of redemption in the book of Exodus. And the questions. The whole night is built to make children ask. There's the famous four questions. There are four children in the Haggadah, the wise one, the rebellious one, the simple one, and the one who doesn't know how to ask, and each gets an answer suited to them. Food is hidden so kids will hunt for it. The rabbis even say: if there's no child, an adult asks. And if you're all alone at the seder, you ask yourself. A freedom that doesn't ask questions, the seder seems to say, isn't finished yet.
screen: `SEDER: ORDER.` · `TELL THY SON IN THAT DAY.` · `MATZAH, BITTER HERBS, SALT WATER.` · `A NIGHT BUILT FOR QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask one real question at dinner. Not how was your day. A real one. For now, settle, and breathe. Think of the people you'll eat with next, or talk to next. What have you never asked them? Where they came from. What they were afraid of as a kid. What they'd want to be free of. Choose one question and hold it ready. The bell holds the time.
Seder. Order: the Passover meal, told in fixed steps, where the story of leaving Egypt is passed on through food and questions.
Your line: ask the questions. Tonight, at dinner or on the phone, ask one person one question you've never asked them, and really listen. Day one hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: On the first night of Passover (and outside Israel, often the second too), Jewish families hold a seder: reading the Haggadah, drinking four cups, eating matzah and bitter herbs, and answering children's questions, including the four questions.

original.note: Hebrew: order; the Passover meal's fixed steps.

trapdoor: what you thought: a big Passover dinner.
what it means: a meal in order where the story of leaving Egypt is told, tasted and questioned, so each person sees themselves in it.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 13:8, 'for me'; Mishnah Pesachim 10:4–5 on the child's questions and seeing oneself as if one left Egypt; four cups for the four promises of Exodus 6:6–7.

sources.quoted: And thou shalt tell thy son in that day, saying: It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt.

notes: 'If alone, ask yourself': Pesachim 116a (a baraita), building on Mishnah Pesachim 10:4. Confirm the attribution 'the Mishnah' vs. 'the Talmud'.
Fifteen steps (Kadesh, Urchatz...) are a medieval mnemonic; phrased 'in the traditional telling'.
Four cups for four expressions of redemption: Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim 10:1. Confirm.
Four questions: the Mishnah's set differs from today's; not detailed.
